Introduction to Computer Language and Flowchart 
 
 
 
 
Learning outcome 
After completing this chapter, students should be able to: 
1. Tell what the characteristics of low-level language are 
2. Tell what the characteristics of high-level language are 
3. Provide example of low-level language

6. Draw flowchart to describe how thing works 
 
 
 
 
Programming Language 
 
A programming language is a set of instructions following a particular           
grammatical rules for instructing computer devices to perform specific tasks. It is            
written by people who are called programmers. Programming Languages are mainly           
classified as low-level and high-level Languages. Low-level language is also called           
“machine language” since it is more understandable by machine rather than human.            
Low-level language consists of byte of instructors and data. Assembly language is a             
good example of such a language. High-level language, on the other hand, is more              
understandable by humans. It was designed to be close to human language, say             
English. As a result, it is a lot easier to learn and comprehend. Some well-known               
high-level languages include Basic, C, Fortran, Pascal, Java, etc. 
At present, most software programmers use high-level languages to create          
application programs because they are easy to write and can be written quicker since              
most projects become more complex and larger scale. However, there are so many             
languages to choose from. It is hard to tell which one is better than the others. One                 
language may be suitable for one particular task, while others may perform better in              
some other task. The choice of language has been an issue to discuss with. Some               
programmers may prefer to stick with a language they have been using for a long               
time. But they may have to switch to use other languages, which can work better on                
their undergoing job than the language they are familiar with. Others may consider             
using a language based on its available development tools. There is no conclusion on              
which language is the best fit on all tasks. In this book, however, C programming               
1

language is considered one of the most popular languages used by programmers. It is              
a core language used in various microcontrollers and very good at creating a variety              
of types of applications. Most people start their first programming skill with C             
language and then extend to other languages such as C++, C#, Java, etc., and other               
web programming languages such as PHP, Javascript and so on. And here are some              
good reasons why C language is prefered by most software developers. 
 
- C language is a very powerful and flexible language. It can be used to create               
projects including operating systems, word processors, graphics, spreadsheets,        
and even compilers for other languages.  
- There are so many useful libraries provided so that it makes the development             
process more efficient. 
- C language was standardized by ANSI (American National Standard Institute),          
which makes the set of rules for C compilers. This helps C language become              
more portable, meaning that a C program can be written on one computer             
system and can be compiled and run on another system. 
- C language is modular and structured programming. The codes can be written            
as functions, which can be called by other parts of a program as many times as                
wished. Additionally, the functions themselve can be reused in other projects           
over and over as well. 
 
There are still some other good sides of C language. This is quite a good               
reason why C language should be used as our first programming language. 
 
 
Types of Programming Language 
 
The main goal of programming languages is to instruct the computer system to             
perform specific tasks according to the statements written in the program. There are             
two main types of programming languages: compiled language and interpreted          
language. 
A compiled language relies on its compiler to translate a source program            
(source code) into machine-understandable code, called executable code, which is          
stored in a binary file. If a source program contains even one error, the translation will                
be aborted and the creation of an executable file is a failure. This means that a                
compiler requires that the source program has to be free of error so that the translation                
process becomes a success. Once the executable file has been created, it can be run               
only on a specific operating system it was compiled into. As a result, an executable               
file used on Microsoft Windows cannot be run on the Mac OS, nor any distributions               
of Linux. Nevertheless, after the successful creation of an executable file, the source             
program is no longer needed, unless the program is fixed or updated and has to be                
recompiled. 
2

An Interpreted language, on the other hand, relies on its interpreter to translate             
the source code into machine-understandable instructions at runtime. This means that           
a source code written in an interpreted language can be run immediately after the code               
has been written. Each statement will be run one-by-one after it has been read by the                
interpreter. If an error is found, the interpretation process stops at the statement that              
causes the error. Since a program written in an interpreted language does not             
transform its source code into an executable file, the source program is always needed              
during the execution.  
A clear difference between these two types is that the compiler performs its             
translation as a whole at once whereas the interpreter performs its translation one             
statement at a time, sometimes called line-by-line translation. Because a compiled           
program is transformed into an executable code, it runs on computer system faster             
than the interpreted program. Therefore, in applications that the execution speed is a             
key factor, the compiled programs are more preferable. However, the interpreted           
programs are quick to create and debug. They are often used to create mockup or               
prototype programs. 
C language is considered as a compiled language because most C language            
vendors make only C compilers to support the development of C programs.  
 
 
History of C Language 
 
C language was first developed by Dennis Ritchie between 1969 and 1973 at             
AT&T Bell Labs. It was used to re-implement the Unix operating system. Ritchie             
called this newly developed language, C, simply because there was already a B             
programming language at his laboratory. C language is easier to understand and code.             
Later, it was used to replace the coding in Assembly language and has since become               
one of the most widely used programming languages of all time. In 1989, C language               
was standardized by ANSI, (ANSI C), and later by ISO (International Organization            
for Standardization). Various vendors distributed their own C compiler such as Turbo            
C, Borland C, CC, Microsoft CL, etc. At the advent of the Linux operating system and                
the open source community, C compiler has since been included in the Linux             
distributions. GNU C Compiler (gcc) is the main building tool used to create the              
Linux operating system itself as well as other applications running on the Linux             
system. The use of C Language is not limited only on desktop computers but it is also                 
used in some other platforms ranging from supercomputers to embedded systems. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3

Compilation Process in C Language 
 
The main purpose of the compilation process is to translate a source program             
into an executable file. But, in fact, this process can be broken down into 4 phases: 1)                 
Pre-processing, 2) Compilation, 3) Assembly, and 4) Linking. 
 
Pre-processing 
In this phase, all comments in the source code are removed. All macros and              
included files are expanded. Given a source file, say hello.c, the preprocessor will             
produce the contents of the header file(s) joined with the contents of the hello.c. In               
this case, a file called hello.i may be created if needed. 
 
Compilation 
This may sound a little confusing by its name, compilation, but it is actually a               
part of the compilation process. In this phase, the preprocessed code (hello.i) is             
translated into assembly level instructions, an intermediate human readable language.          
Because of this phase, it is legal to add inline assembly instructions in a C coding                
program. The output file of this phase is hello.s. However, some compilers employ an              
integrated assembler, which skips the generation of the intermediate assembly          
instructions and directly creates machine code instead. 
 
Assembly 
In this phase, the intermediate assembly instruction (hello.s) is given as input            
and will be translated by assembler into machine level instructions. This phase            
generates an object file, hello.o, which actually contains the instructions to be run on              
the target processor. 
 
Linking 
This is the final phase at which the executable file is generated. In this phase,               
Linker performs some extra work by rearranging the object codes that are out of order               
or missing. Linker locates where the functions are implemented so that they can be              
called by other pieces of codes. It also adds some code which is required when the                
program starts and ends. Some added code is responsible for setting up the             
environment like passing command line arguments. If all works well, the target            
executable file is created and, finally, this is the end of the whole compilation              
process. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4

Flowchart Diagram 
 
What is a flowchart? 
A flowchart is an organized combination of shapes, lines, and text that            
graphically illustrates a process or structure. Flowchart plays an important part in            
learning programming because it employs graphical representation to simplify the          
steps of the programming process This makes it easier for programming learners to             
understand program’s operations and translate it into a coding program. Since           
flowchart is language-independent, it can be used in any languages of choice. 
 
Use of Flowchart 
A flowchart can be used to define and analyze processes. For example, we can              
describe a registration process for new freshman students. The pictorial representation           
is more intuitive and understandable than that of the textual presentation. In addition,             
using a step-by-step picture of the process can shorten the time for discussing and              
communicating among team members. 
Flowcharts are recognized as one of the most important tools to reduce a gap              
between people with different knowledge backgrounds, educations, and positions.         
People may spend hours of talking, discussing, and coming up with a conclusion on              
what they are trying to complete. Flowchart is a universal language that can put              
everybody on the same page and make things done quicker. Once a flowchart is              
completed, it can be used for training, troubleshooting, testing, and inspecting           
processes. 
 
Flowchart Symbol Definition 
There are a variety of flowchart symbol definitions. They may be slightly            
different on some particular symbols. However, they share more common features           
than different ones. The most important thing to remember is when using these             
symbols, we have to be consistent with their meanings. The common flowchart            
symbols  used in the programming process and their meaning are given in Table 1-1.

Chapter 2 
Introduction to C Programming 
 
 
 
 
Learning outcome 
After completing this chapter, students should be able to: 
1. Write a program to use directive macro to import a header file 
2. Create an executable file using a C compiler 
3. Tell how to declare a variable according to identifier naming rules 
4. Write a program using arithmetic operators 
 
 
 
 
Header File, Preprocessing, and ​#include​ Directive 
 
C implementation provides​header filescontaining the necessary declarations         
for various parts of the library. For example, the header file ​math.h contains             
declarations for mathematical functions, the header file​stdio.h contains declarations          
for standard input and output functions. 
 
The C compiler provides a simple way of effectively inserting header files into             
a source file, which can be controlled with​preprocessing directives​, all of which             
begin with the symbol ​#​. 
 
An ​#include directive designates a file whose contents are to be inserted into             
the program text. When the preprocessor encounters an​#include directive​, it replaces            
the directive by the contents of the designated file. 
 
An example of how to use ​stdio​ library is shown below: 
 
#include <stdio.h> 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
10

Printing String to Computer Screen 
 
The library function​printf() is a powerful function for formatting and printing            
output. The functions in​stdio.h access input and output devices via streams. Each             
stream is connected to a source of destination for data, such as a keyboard, a display,                
a printer, or a disk file. The function​printf() writes data to the standard output stream,                
stdout​, which is normally connected to the user’s display monitor. Some examples of             
how to use ​printf()​ are given below: 
 
printf(“abc”); 
printf(“def”); 
printf(“ghi”); 
 
The result from executing the above statements are given below. 
 
abcdefghi 
 
Note​: ​printf() does not automatically cause the new line after a string has been              
printed. If we wish the strings to be printed on separate lines, we must include               
new-line characters in the string literals as follows. 
 
printf(“abc\n”); 
printf(“def\n”); 
printf(“ghi\n”); 
 
These statements produce the output as 
 
abc 
def 
ghi 
 
An alternative, simpler, way to do so is to incorporate the new-line characters             
into a single statement as: 
 
printf(“abc\ndef\nghi\n”); 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
12

Editing, Compiling, Linking, Executing, and Debugging 
 
The text of a C program is stored in one or more source files, which can be                 
created and revised with the aid of a text editor, such as​notepad (in Windows),​vi or                 
gedit​ (in Linux), etc. 
We use a​C compilerto translate each source file into a machine-coded object              
file. Each source file is compiled separately. 
The ​linker combines the object files with one another and with the code for              
any library functions called by the program. The output from the linker is an              
executable file, which contains all the machine code for the program and is ready to               
be run on the target computer. 
Here, we use ​gcc​ to compile the hello.c on Linux: 
 
$gcc -c hello.c 
 
The option -c given above tells gcc to create an object file from the source file.                
We get hello.o as the​object filefrom the above compilation. Then, we link the object                
file (in this case, we have just one file) to produce an executable file. The -o indicates                 
the executable file to be produced named “​hello​”. 
 
$gcc hello.o -o hello 
 
We can now execute the program as follow: 
 
$./hello 
 
After executing, the result is given as shown below. 
Hello World! 
 
If we have only a single source file to be compiled, we may not need to                
generate the object file. This can simply be done by using: 
 
$gcc hello.c -o hello 
 
which produces the same result as the above operations. (Except that the object file              
will not be created.)  
However, we can use a short command as​$gcc hello.c​, which will produce a              
default executable file named ​a.out​. We may then type ​$./a.out​ to run it.  
Note​: If we encounter any problems during the compilation, we may need to edit              
(​debug​) the program. Even if the program may have passed the compilation, it may              
produce undesirable output. In this case, we might need some debugging tools, i.e.             
gdb​, to correct the problems. 
13

Identifier 
 
In C programming, the identifiers (variables and functions) must be formed           
according to certain rules: 
 
● An identifier can contain only letters, digits, and the underscore character, _. 
● An identifier must begin with a letter of the alphabet or an underscore             
character. Thus ​_func_call​ is a valid identifier but ​1st_round​ is ​not​. 
● An identifier must not be the same as one of the ​keywords​ in C. 
● C distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters, so that​amount​,          
Amount​, and ​AMOUNT​ are three different identifiers. 
● An identifier defined by programmer should not be the same as one already             
defined in the library. For example, ​printf should not be used as a             
programmer-defined identifier. 
 
 
Variable and Assignment 
 
A ​variable is a memory location named by an identifier. The value stored in              
the memory location is the current​value of the variable​. This value can be changed by                
an ​assignment operation, which stores a new value in the memory location. The             
following declarations 
 
int count; 
double amount; 
 
declare ​count as integer variable and ​amount as double variable. We can declare             
several variables of the same type in a single declaration as: 
 
int i, j, k; 
double w, x, y, z; 
 
We can give an initial value to a variable with an equal sign to the variable we want to                   
declare. 
 
int count = 100; 
double amount = 29.95; 
Likewise, 
 
int i = 10, j = 20, k = 30; 
is an example of multiple initializations to multiple variables. 
 
14

Declarations in a block (a pair of braces {...}) should be given before the              
statements. For example, the block 
 
{ 
int count = 100; 
double amount = 29.95; 
 
count = 150; 
amount = 49.95; 
} 
 
declares ​count​ and ​amount​, then assigns new value to each variable. 
 
Variables declared within a block are called​local variables​. A local variable            
can be referred to only from within the block in which it is declared. Such variables                
cannot be used outside the block they are declared in. 
 
Built-in data types provided by C language are listed in Table 2-1. 
 
   Table 2-1.​ Built-in data types in C language 
Data Type Size in byte Description 
char 1 A character or one-byte integer 
short 2 Small integer number 
int 4 Integer number

long long 4 Big integer number

Note: any integer types are signed numbers. We can place the keyword            
“​unsigned​” in front of them to use them as positive numbers such as​unsigned char​,               
unsigned short​, ​unsigned int​, and​ unsigned long​. 
 
 
 
15

Expression 
 
An expression is anything that evaluates to a numeric value. A simple            
expression may consist of a single item such as a simple variable, literal constant, or               
symbolic constant. An example of each simple expression is shown in Table 2-2. 
 
 
          ​Table 2-2.​ Simple expressions 
Expression Description 
MAX A symbolic constant 
10 A literal constant 
x a variable 
 
 
A symbolic constant evaluates to the value it is given in the#define directive.              
A literal constant evaluates to its own value. A variable evaluates to the value it is                
currently stored. 
An expression may consist of a combination of more simple expressions,           
which normally are connected by one or more operators. This is called “complex             
expression”. The expression  
 
x * 10  
 
is composed of two simple expressions, a variable​x and a literal constant​10​, which               
are connected by multiplication operator​*​. If the value of​x is 2, then the expression                
x * 10 evaluates to 20. A complex expression may get even more complex as               
x * x + x - 2​. In many cases, complex expression contains assignment operation such                
as 
 
y = x + 10; 
 
This statement first evaluates the expression​x + 10and then assigns the result to​y​.                
In this case, the assignment operator tells that the left side of the equal sign is to                 
evaluate. Since this statement is also an expression, it evaluates to the value of​y​.               
If  ​x​ is given as 10, the expression evaluates to 20. 
 
 
 
 
17

Operator 
 
An operator is a symbol that instructs C programming to perform some            
operation or action on one or more operands. An operand is an expression referring to               
something that an operator acts on. The fundamental operators in C programming            
include assignment operator and arithmetic operator. 
 
Assignment operator 
C programming uses equal sign, =, to indicate the assignment operator. A            
simple form of assignment is given as: 
 
variable = expression; 
 
which is that after the expression has been evaluated, the result will be assigned to the                
variable on the left side. An example of an assignment statement is 
 
a = 10; 
 
which means assigning the value of literal constant 10 to variable ​a​. Or an              
assignment statement  
 
of 
 
a = b; 
 
means assigning the value of​b to ​a​. (​Keeping in mind​that, in C programming, this is                 
not an evaluation of whether x is equal to y.​) 
 
Arithmetic Operator 
The arithmetic operators in C programming take two operands to perform a            
particular operation, which is called binary arithmetic operators. The common          
arithmetic operators are shown in Table 2-3. 
 
Table 2-3.​ Arithmetic Operations 
Integer Types Floating Types 
  +  addition 
  -   subtraction 
  *  multiplication 
  /   integer division: quotient 
  % integer division: remainder 
  +  addition 
  -   subtraction 
  *  multiplication 
  /   floating-point division 
 
18

When +, -, and * are applied to two integers, the operation is carried out using                
integer arithmetic, and the result is an integer. If either or both operands are              
floating-point numbers, the operation is carried out using floating-point arithmetic,          
and the result is a floating-point number 
The effect of the division operation, /, differs for integer and floating-point            
operands. If both operands are integers, / computes only the integer quotient; the             
remainder is discarded. Thus, the value of​9/2 is 4. If either or both operands are                
floating-point numbers, a floating-point division is done. Thus, ​9/2.0​, ​9.0/2​, and           
9.0/2.0​ are 4.5. 
The ​% operation, ​modulus​, computes the remainder of two integers. For           
example, ​9%2​ evaluates to 1, at which ​9%3​ evaluates to 0. 
Arithmetic operators may take only a single operand. It is called unary            
arithmetic operators, which is shown in Table 2-4. 
 
Table 2-4.​ Unary Arithmetic operators 
Operator Name Action 
++ Increment Increase the value of operand by one 
-- Decrement Decrease the value of operand by one 
 
The operand of unary arithmetic operators can only be an integer variable. The             
value of the operand is added or subtracted by 1. The statements of 
 
x++;  
and 
++x; 
 
are equivalent to the statement 
 
x = x + 1; 
 
From the statements above, it can be seen that the unary operator can be              
placed before (​prefix​) or after (​postfix​) the operand. The difference of these two             
modes is when the value is incremented or decremented. The prefix operator will             
update the value after the operand before it is used while the postfix operator will               
update the operand value after it is used. The following statements are a good              
example of how the prefix operator works. 
 
x = 10; 
y = x++; 
printf(“x = %d and y = %d\n”, x, y); 
19

In the​printf() ​statement, the value of​x is 11 while the value of​y is 10. This is because                    
when ​x is assigned toy​, its value is equal to 10. After the assignment is done, the                  
value of ​x is incremented by 1. As a result, the printed values are “​x = 11 and y =                    
10​”. 
 
 
Precedence of Arithmetic Operators 
 
In complex expressions, the order in which operation should be performed           
first is very important to the result from a calculation. Each operator has its own               
priority. The operator precedence is given in Table 2-5. 
 
 
       Table 2-5.​ The precedence of arithmetic operators 
Operator Precedence 
++ -- 1 
* / % 2 
+ - 3 
 
 
From Table 2-5, it can seen that unary operators have highest priority while             
the addition and subtraction have lowest priority. Thus the statement 
 
x = 2 + 3 * 5; 
 
will evaluate​3 * 5first. The result of the evaluation (15) is then added to 2 giving a                   
result of 17 being assigned to​x​. However, in some cases, we may need to perform                
addition before multiplication. This can be done by enclosing the addition operation            
by parentheses. Therefore, the statement 
 
x = (2 + 3) * 5; 
 
will assign 25 to ​x​.

Chapter 3 
Input and Output 
 
 
 
 
Learning outcome 
After completing this chapter, students should be able to: 
1. Write a program to print data of each data type to computer screen 
2. Write a program to receive data of each data type from keyboard 
3. Print floating point numbers with assigned precision 
4. Print formatted data to computer screen using field-width justification 
 
 
 
 
The standard input/output library (stdio.h) provides a number of input and           
output functions. The most generally useful functions are ​printf() for output and            
scanf() for input. Function printf() displays formatted string to standard output           
(stdout), which is computer screen. Function scanf(), on the other hand, receives data             
of specified type from standard input (stdin), which is computer keyboard. 
 
 
Output with ​printf() 
 
From the previous chapter, we can see that​printf() needs string as its argument              
to be printed to the computer screen. However, if we would like to print a number, we                 
can simply add an additional argument to the function. Thus, the first argument of              
printf() is called​format string​, which can contain​conversion specificationsdescribing           
how other values are to be converted into printed form. The values to be converted are                
supplied as additional arguments. When the format string is printed, each conversion            
specification is replaced by the corresponding converted value. 
A conversion specification always begins with a ​% sign. The simplest           
conversion specifications for the data types are listed in Table 3-1. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
23

Table 3-1.​ Conversion specification for data type 
Conversion Specification Data Type 
%d, %i int 
%f float and double 
%lf double 
%c char 
%s char[] or char* (string) 
%lu unsigned int 
%p Address of a variable 
 
 
It is also possible that a number may need to be represented in other forms.               
The conversion specification ​%o prints out numbers in octal decimal format, while            
%x​ represents numbers in hexadecimal format. 
 
An example of printf constant number using conversion specification format is given            
as 
 
printf(“%d plus %d equals %d.\n”, 20, 30, 50); 
 
, which prints out as 
 
20 plus 30 equals 50. 
 
The arguments of printf() can be represented by variables or expressions. For            
example, the statements 
 
x = 2.5; 
y = 3.5; 
printf(“The product is %f.\n”, x * y); 
 
will print out 
 
The product is 8.750000. 
24

The result from executing this program is shown below.

Typewriter     249.98 
Paper          5.99 
 
Note​: “\t can be used as a tab in the format string”. 
 
 
Input with ​scanf() 
 
The input function​scanf() is similar to​printf() in that input is controlled by a               
format string. The function ​printf() writes conversion specification to the standard           
output stream (​stdout​), while ​scanf() reads conversion specification from the standard           
input stream (​stdin​)​,​ which is connected to the user's keyboard. 
One distinction is that ​printf() takes variable as its argument while ​scanf()            
takes ​the address of variable​, which is represented as an ampersand sign, ​&​,             
preceding the variable. For example, the statements 
 
int x; 
scanf(“%d”, &x); 
 
reads an integer number and stores it in the variable ​x​. Likewise, the statement 
 
scanf(“%d%d%d”, &i, &j, &k); 
 
reads three integers from standard input stream, converts them into type​int​, and stores              
them in variables ​i, j, and ​k​, respectively. Values to be read are separated by               
whitespace, which can consist of spaces, tabs, and newlines.

What is a file? 
 
C language was originated from UNIX, at which it treats each device (disk,             
keyboard, screen, printer, etc.) in the system as a file. In order to read from or write                 
to a file, we firstly need to open it. Then, data can be transferred from a program to                  
the opened file, or from the file to the program. The flow of transferred data is called                 
“​stream​”. Thus, working with a file I/O, we need to create a stream to a specific file.                 
Essentially, after the data transfer is completed, the opened file needs to be closed. 
 
 
Types of file 
 
Generally, there are two types of files:​text and ​binary​. A text file refers to a                
file that contains a sequence of characters (ASCII data), while a binary file contains a               
series of binary data. A text file stored textual data, readable by humans, at which               
each line is separated by a newline character (“​\n​”). Text files can be opened with any                
text editors. In order to communicate with a text file, a textual stream is needed. A                
binary file, on the other hand, stores non-textual data, which are composed of a series               
of bytes and unreadable by humans. Some binary files can be executed by the system               
(.exe) while some contain data, which will be used by other programs. Some             
examples of binary files include picture files such as​.jpg, .png, .gif, .bmp, .tif​, etc.,               
document files such as​.doc, .pdf, .rtf,​etc, or media files such as.mp3, .mp4, .mov,                
wma, wmv​, etc. Each of these files needs designated application programs to open and              
manipulate it. In order to communicate with a binary file, a binary stream is needed.

File Stream 
 
We can declare a stream of a file as a pointer to​FILE ​object. The following                
example shows how to declare a variable of file pointer, which will be used to transfer                
data between program and file. 
 
FILE  *fptr; 
 
File pointer variable​fptr ​is a stream to a file that can be used to read data from                  
or write data to the opened file. File pointer can be either text or binary stream,                
depending on how we set it.  
 
 
 
Open a Stream to File 
 
Before any transfer can proceed, a file must be opened first. A library function              
fopen()​, in ​stdio.h​, is used to open a text file or binary file depending on which mode                 
we want to use. The prototype function of ​fopen()​ is given below: 
 
FILE  *fopen(const char *filename, const char *mode); 
 
On successful open, ​fopen() returns a FILE pointer representing the stream.           
Otherwise, it returns a​NULL ​pointer if it fails to do so. Function​fopen() requires two                
arguments. The first argument is a filename, which is a string representing the file to               
be opened. The second argument is an open mode, which specifies properties of the              
stream. The details of how a file will be opened is given in Table 11-1.

Error Handling for fopen() 
 
There may be some cases that a file cannot be opened. For example, if we               
attempt to open a file that does not exist for reading,​fopen() will return a ​NULL                
pointer to indicate that a stream file cannot be established. This causes an error to the                
program. It is impossible to proceed with reading data. Thus, it is very important that               
we should check for an error occurrence on opening a file. The following example              
shows a simple way to check whether fopen() is successful. 
 
fptr = fopen(“input.txt”, “r”); 
if(fptr == NULL) { 
printf(“Error: cannot open file”); 
return EXIT_FAILURE; // return 1; 
} 
 
From the example above, if the file is opened successfully, the program can             
proceed with reading data from the file. On the other hand, if the ​fopen() is               
unsuccessful, the program should terminate itself. Any operations on this file should            
not be done. Terminating the program is a wise choice to choose. However, it is a                
good idea that the program should notify the user of what is happening before              
terminating itself.

Close the File Stream 
 
After file operations are over, the opened file should be closed. This will             
return the control over the file back to the operating system. In addition, it can prevent                
unexpected effects from any upcoming usages of this file by other processes. The             
function prototype of closing a file stream is given below. 
 
int fclose(FILE *stream); 
 
Function ​fclose() will return 0, if the file stream is closed successfully.            
Otherwise, it will return EOF. An example of closing a file stream is illustrated              
below. 
 
int result = fclose(fptr); 
 
After a call of​fclose()​, the value of​fptr ​is no longer valid. It must not be used                  
for any read/write operation thereafter. However, it can be used to open a file again.

Manipulating Direct Access 
 
Working with files in sequential mode can be tedious and burdensome. It is             
more convenient to be able to control the file pointer. The abilities to locate file               
pointer and move it around are necessary for direct access. The current position of a               
file pointer can be obtained from function​ftell()​, at which its function prototype is              
given below. 
 
long  ftell(FILE *stream); 
 
Function ftell() requires file stream argument and returns the current position           
of the file pointer in terms of long integer. 
For moving the file pointer to the desired position, C programming provides            
fseek()​ to perform this operation. The function prototype of ​fseek()​ is given below. 
 
int fseek(FILE *stream, long offset, int mode); 
 
Function ​fseek() ​requires 3 arguments: file stream, offset, and mode. The           
function moves the file pointer to the offset value according to the mode given in               
Table 11-2. It returns 0 if the pointer has been moved successfully. Otherwise, it              
returns a nonzero integer if an error occurs. 
 
  Table 11-2.​ File seek mode 
Mode Value Description 
SEEK_SET 0 Offset is from the beginning of the file. 
SEEK_CUR 1 Offset is from the current position. 
SEEK_END 2 Offset is from the end of the file. 
 
In order to move the file pointer to the beginning of the file, C programming               
provides function ​rewind() to perform such operation. The function prototype of           
rewind()​ is given below. 
 
void rewind(FILE *stream); 
 
Function ​rewind() requires the specific file stream as its argument. It does not             
return a value. However, this function is equivalent to using fseek(stream, 0L,            
SEEK_SET), which also moves file pointer to position 0 from the beginning of the              
file (SEEK_SET mode).

Learning outcome

“​C language is modular​” meaning that C programming is based on functions.            
In a large project, a source file may be full of functions. This does not make                
modularity more efficient. The codes become too complex, resulting in reducing the            
readability. Code inspection will also be very difficult to locate an issue that may              
cause a problem to the program. A better way to work around this problem is to break                 
the source file into smaller multiple files. In function​main()​, we can import functions              
from other source files, and make a call to them as needed. Thus, any errors that                
might arise in the project will be isolated making it easier to locate the problem. In                
addition, this will also improve the modularity of the program. 
C programming allows us to keep functions in separate files. These file can be              
imported for use in our program using directive​#include​. Furthermore, the interfaces            
of functions (function prototypes) and their implementations can be stored separately.           
Traditionally, the function prototypes and variable declarations are kept in a header            
file (​.h file​), while the function implementations are kept in a source file (​.c​ ​file​).  
The following example illustrates how a C project can be created. The project             
structure consists of 3 files: a header file containing function prototypes shown in             
Lising 12-1, a source file containing the implementations of all functions defined in             
the header file shown in Listing 12-2, and a main source file containing function              
main() to launch the execution and all main control of the program shown in Listing               
12-3.  
 
/* File:  arith.h  /* 
// Header file containing function prototypes 
int add(int, int); 
int subtract(int, int); 
 
Listing 12-1.​ Header file (arith.h)

In order to make an executable file, all the source files must be compiled and               
linked together. In this case, we have two source files,​arith.c and ​main.c​. Both must               
be compiled to create object files. Then, both object files must be linked together so               
that all the functions can be located. The executable file from the above project can be                
created by using ​gcc​ as follows: 
 
1. Compile all source files to generate object files: 
 
$gcc -c arith.c main.c 
 
This ​-c​ option tells ​gcc ​to generate ​arith.o​ and ​main.o 
 
2. Link all object files together to generate an executable file 
 
$gcc arith.o main.o -o main 
 
This command lets ​gcc ​link the object files together. The -o option tells ​gcc ​to 
generate an executable file named main. If the ​-o​ and the target file name are omitted, 
the executable file will automatically be named ​a.out​ on Linux and ​a.exe​ on 
Windows.  
(​Note​:​ the commands will be different on different compilers.) 
 
In a large project, there may be so many header and source files to keep track                
with. It is possible that a header file may be included more than once. Consequently,               
the compiler will compile its contents more than once. As a result, the compiler gives               
out an error because of the duplicate contents. A typical approach to deal with this               
problem is to enclose the entire contents in the header file with a conditional              
preprocessor directive as shown in Listing 12-4. 
 
 
 
/* File:  arith.h  (new arith.h) */ 
// Header file with conditional directive 
#ifndef ARITH_H 
#define ARITH_H 
int add(int, int); 
int subtract(int, int); 
#endif 
 
Listing 12-4.​ Modified Header file 
 
106

The preprocessor directive​#ifndef checks whether a macro name (​ARITH_H​)          
has not been defined. On the first read,​ARITH_H has not yet been defined. Therefore,               
it is defined here and all subsequent contents are read. Later, if this header file is                
included again, it first checks for the Macro name,​ARITH_H​, which has just been              
defined previously. As a result, all contents within ​#ifndef​ block will be skipped.
